opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's funny, because I think for a lot of people my age the path into deep learning went through Lua Torch. When I started, I was coming from a more traditional NLP background, structured prediction, dynamic programming, parsing, that kind of thing. And I remember picking up Torch and just being struck by how it changed the unit of thinking. Instead of writing a whole bespoke system for each model, you were composing modules. You could take a little piece, a lookup table, an LSTM, a linear layer, snap them together, and actually run something on a GPU in an afternoon. That was a real shift in what felt possible for a small group.

Then PyTorch came along and took that idea and made it feel native. The define-by-run style, eager execution, just writing Python and having the gradients work, meant the code you wrote looked a lot like the math you had in your head. And I think that matters more than people give it credit for. When the gap between the idea and the implementation shrinks, you start to think differently. You try more things. You debug by poking at tensors instead of staring at a graph compiler error. Research became much more experimental and iterative, almost like a lab science.

For teaching, it was huge. I used to spend a lot of class time on infrastructure, on how to get anything to train at all. With PyTorch, students could get to the interesting part much faster. But it also made me realize there's a risk: if everything is just `loss.backward()`, students can treat it as magic. So a lot of what I've tried to do since, things like MiniTorch or various puzzles, is go the other direction and have people build the core pieces themselves: autodiff, tensors, broadcasting, even a little bit of the GPU side. Because once you've built a toy version, you really understand what the library is doing for you, and you get much better at using it and at knowing when it's going to bite you.

So I'd say Torch taught me that modularity changes research culture, and PyTorch taught me that good abstractions are a kind of pedagogy. The tool itself shapes how a whole generation of people thinks about models. That's a big responsibility, and it's also why I think it's worth teaching what's underneath.

r001.rationale: The response says PyTorch let him write Python that looked a lot like the math in his head, with gradients working.

r002.rationale: It describes using MiniTorch to have students build core components such as autodiff and tensors, explaining that building a toy version helps them understand the library.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so my path into this is a little unusual, because I came to Torch pretty late, and actually somewhat reluctantly. When I was doing my PhD, most of what I did was in the structured prediction world—dynamic programs, inference algorithms, a lot of hand-written code in Java and C++. Neural nets were something other people did. So when I ended up spending time with people at Facebook around 2014, 2015, I was basically forced to learn Lua Torch, and I remember being kind of annoyed about it. Lua is a strange language, the ecosystem was small, and I had this attitude of "I already know how to write gradients, why do I need this?"

But what Torch did for me, and this is the part I didn't anticipate, is that it made the whole thing feel like a programming problem rather than a math problem. In the structured prediction world, you'd spend weeks deriving a model, deriving the inference, deriving the gradient, and then you'd write code that was essentially a transcription of a paper. If you wanted to change something, you'd go back to the whiteboard. Torch, and then much more so PyTorch, collapsed that cycle. You write the forward computation the way you'd write any program, and the gradient is just handled. So the question stopped being "can I derive this" and became "what do I want to compute." That sounds like a small shift but for me it was enormous. It changed what kinds of ideas I was willing to try, because the cost of trying was so low.

And then PyTorch specifically, with the eager, Pythonic style, mattered a lot because it meant the code looked like what you'd write on a whiteboard anyway. There's this nice correspondence where a line of PyTorch is more or less a line of math. That's what pushed me toward things like the Annotated Transformer, where the entire premise is that the paper and the code can sit side by side and you don't need a translation layer between them. I don't think I would have done that with the earlier tooling because there was always too much scaffolding in the way.

On the teaching side, it honestly flipped how I think about what a course is for. I used to teach NLP the way I was taught—here's the model, here's the derivation, go implement it. And students would spend most of their time fighting with indexing bugs or getting a gradient slightly wrong, and that's not really the thing you want them to learn. Once PyTorch existed, I could say: the mechanics are handled, so let's actually spend the time on the ideas. Why attention? What are the inductive biases? What breaks when you scale? And the homework becomes something closer to real research—build this thing, run it, look at what it does.

The other piece, which I've come to care about a lot, is that PyTorch made it possible to teach by reading code. I've always learned best from reading other people's implementations, and historically that was hard in ML because the implementations were either enormous research codebases or little demos that didn't actually work. PyTorch produced this middle ground where a serious model could be a few hundred readable lines. So a lot of what I do now—the tutorials, the puzzles, the "let's implement this from scratch" exercises—really comes from that realization that if the code is small enough and clear enough, the code is the explanation.

I'd add one caveat, which is that there's a cost to this too. Having everything be so easy means people sometimes don't learn what's happening underneath. I think about that a lot with the GPU puzzles and the Tensor Puzzles stuff—it's partly me trying to push back a little and say, the abstraction is wonderful, but you should still be able to peel it back when you need to. So I guess the honest answer is that Torch taught me how much the tooling shapes the research, and PyTorch taught me that the same tooling can shape how people learn, and I've spent a good chunk of the last several years trying to take advantage of that.

r001.rationale: The response says PyTorch code has a close correspondence to math—“a line of PyTorch is more or less a line of math”—and describes it as letting him focus on what he wanted to compute.

r002.rationale: The response mentions tutorials, puzzles, and implementing models from scratch, but does not describe a MiniTorch approach in which students build their own small version of PyTorch.

astra-6.text:
Learning Torch made a lot of ideas concrete for me. You can understand a model on paper, but implementing it forces you to understand how the pieces fit together. And once you can change those pieces and see what happens, implementation becomes part of how you think through a research question.

PyTorch also made that way of thinking much easier to bring into teaching. You could write code that looked reasonably close to the mathematical description, run it, and inspect the intermediate results. So instead of presenting the equations and then treating implementation as a separate exercise, you could move back and forth between them. That’s a powerful way to learn: you make a prediction about what a model should do, try it, and figure out why your understanding was incomplete.

r001.rationale: The candidate says PyTorch let him write code that looked reasonably close to the mathematical description, expressing the idea that research math could be translated almost directly into code.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses teaching through implementing and inspecting models, but does not mention MiniTorch or students building their own small version of PyTorch.

sol-6.1.text:
Learning Torch made neural networks feel much more concrete to me. You could take an idea from a paper, implement it, and see what it actually did. And the implementation would expose things that the equations didn’t necessarily make clear—what the assumptions were, where the computation was happening, what was difficult to optimize.

PyTorch made that connection even more direct because you could write something that looked like ordinary Python and differentiate through it. That changed how I thought about teaching. You could put the mathematical description next to a small piece of code, and students could modify it and build intuition by experimenting. Research and teaching started to feel much closer: in both cases, you’re trying to turn an abstract idea into something you can inspect, question, and understand.

r001.rationale: The response says PyTorch let Sasha write ordinary Python that could be differentiated and connect mathematical descriptions directly to code, conveying near-direct expression of research ideas in code.

r002.rationale: The response discusses teaching through small code students can modify, but does not mention MiniTorch or having students build their own small PyTorch implementation.
